pages.title: Read the situation
pages.instruction: Read the account and identify what happened and what is still unknown
pages.subject: The learner’s priorities
paragraphs: The learner wants feedback on a practical project. Wednesday evenings and a Friday check-in usually fit their schedule; Tuesday is a fixed commitment. A lower fee is attractive, but they can consider paying more for feedback that applies directly to the project.
Finishing sooner would be useful, although there is no firm completion deadline. The learner still needs to check whether either timetable might change and how the project feedback is provided.

pages.title: Read the situation
pages.instruction: Read the account and identify what happened and what is still unknown
pages.subject: The two course offers
paragraphs: Course A costs $180 and lasts eight weeks. Its advertised sessions run on Wednesdays from 7 to 9 pm, with practical tasks and feedback during class.

Course B costs $320 and lasts twelve weeks. It combines independent work with a Friday 6 pm check-in, when the learner’s project is discussed. Neither offer guarantees that its timetable will stay unchanged.

pages.title: Link changes with the more … the more
pages.instruction: Use a comparative in each half to connect two changes

rows.subject: Two increases
rows.verb: The more + clause, the more + clause
rows.example: The more I practise, the more confident I feel

rows.subject: An increase and a decrease
rows.verb: The more + clause, the less + clause
rows.example: The more time I spend commuting, the less time I have to study

rows.subject: Other comparatives
rows.verb: The + comparative + clause, the + comparative + clause
rows.example: The earlier I finish, the easier it is to attend

pages.note: Both halves need a comparative. The is part of this construction: the more, the less, the earlier. It does not mean that the relationship has been proved in every situation.

pages.title: Listen and answer
pages.instruction: A preference becomes a constraint. Listen for the new information and decide how to respond
pages.message: Hi, Ana. Course A has changed its live session from Wednesday to Tuesday, still seven to nine. The person on our brief has a regular Tuesday commitment and cannot attend live then. The provider also says the practical feedback is only given during that live class, not on a recording afterwards. The price and eight-week length are unchanged. This turns attendance from a flexible preference into a serious constraint. Course B’s Friday check-in still fits, but we should confirm whether its feedback covers the person’s project before accepting the higher cost. Could you explain how the balance has changed rather than simply saying the more expensive course is now better? There may also be a later run of A worth asking about
